questions.question: List the hazards faced by a fire fighter and by an NSRI sea rescue volunteer, and state the textile property that each hazard demands.
questions.expected_answer: A fire fighter faces flame, which demands flame resistance from a fabric that neither catches fire nor melts onto skin; radiant heat, which demands insulation and a reflective or heat-resistant outer; hot water and steam, which demand a water and steam barrier; falling debris and sharp edges, which demand tear and abrasion resistance; and sweat and heat from exertion inside the suit, which demand breathability and ventilation. An NSRI volunteer faces cold water, which drains body heat twenty-five times faster than air and demands insulation that works when wet; waves and the risk of going overboard, which demand buoyancy that keeps the head up; darkness, which demands fluorescent colour and retroreflective tape; wind, spray and salt, which demand waterproofing with sealed seams and corrosion-resistant fittings; and the need to swim and climb, which demands stretch and low weight. All protective clothing must also be comfortable and wearable for hours, so weight and fit are specifications.

questions.question: Compare the properties of natural and synthetic fibres relevant to protective clothing, and explain how weaving, knitting, coating, laminating and finishing give fabrics their properties, with the results of the swatch tests.
questions.expected_answer: Cotton is soft, absorbent and cool but weak when wet, slow to dry and quick to burn, though it burns to ash rather than melting; wool insulates even when damp because its crimped fibres trap air and it chars slowly and self-extinguishes, but it is heavy when wet. Polyester is strong, quick-drying and stable but melts in flame and sticks to skin; nylon is very strong, abrasion-resistant and light but also melts; aramids such as the fibre sold as Nomex char without melting and keep strength in heat, and the fibre sold as Kevlar is far stronger than steel by weight and cut-resistant. Weaving interlaces threads at right angles for strong, stable, low-stretch cloth such as canvas and jacket shells; knitting loops yarn so fabric stretches and traps air, as in fleece and thermal wear; bonding makes felt and wadding. Coating with PVC or polyurethane makes fabric waterproof and windproof; laminating a membrane with pores too small for drops but large enough for vapour makes it waterproof and breathable; flame-retardant treatment protects cotton; fluorescent dye and retroreflective tape give visibility. In tests cotton soaks water, tears easily and flares; polyester beads water briefly, resists tearing and melts to a bead; coated nylon sheds water completely; wool chars and goes out; aramid barely tears and chars without melting; reflective tape glows back at a torch.

questions.question: Describe how a fire fighter's turnout jacket and an NSRI volunteer's outfit are built in layers, explaining the job of each layer, and state the general layering principle.
questions.expected_answer: The turnout jacket has an outer shell of tightly woven aramid blend that resists flame, does not melt, resists tearing and carries reflective trim; a moisture barrier of membrane laminated to light fabric that keeps hot water and steam from the body while letting some sweat vapour out; and an innermost thermal liner of quilted or non-woven aramid wadding that traps air, the best insulator, to slow heat reaching the skin, the whole weighing several kilograms and needing ventilation against heat stress. The NSRI outfit has a wicking thermal base layer of polyester or merino wool that insulates when damp, a knitted fleece mid-layer that traps air, an outer of PVC-coated or laminated nylon with taped or welded seams, high collar, hood and sealing cuffs, and over everything a life jacket of closed-cell foam or an inflatable bladder in a tough fluorescent nylon cover with retroreflective patches, whistle and light that keeps an unconscious person face up; in the coldest water a drysuit sealed at neck and wrists or a neoprene wetsuit is worn. The general principle is an outer layer against the weather, a middle layer that insulates, an inner layer that manages moisture and comfort, and seams and fastenings that do not leak, which also applies to an emergency shelter.
